title: Pawnee Commons

jokes.text: Radio sponsorship announcement for 'The Shadows of Seven Heads' — 'the dramic tale of an Israeli soldier who falls in love with conjoined Palestinian sextuplets.'
jokes.setup: A routine public-radio sponsorship read, mimicking the dry, earnest tone of NPR underwriting announcements.
jokes.punchline: The film described is maximally absurd — 'dramic,' conjoined sextuplets, an Israeli-Palestinian romance — delivered with total deadpan sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The joke earns its high score by layering absurdity precisely: 'dramic' (a malapropism), conjoined sextuplets (escalating specificity), and the geopolitical sensitivity of the pairing — all delivered in the flattest possible public-radio voice. The specificity of 'Focus Features' adds a real-world anchor that makes the absurdity land harder. Strong originality and economy.

jokes.text: Derry Murbles explains he is 'sitting in for Nina Joplin, who is touring the country performing a spoken-word opera about pear-shaped women.'
jokes.setup: Standard public-radio host introduction explaining a guest host.
jokes.punchline: The reason the regular host is absent is an utterly specific, absurd performance art project described with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Follows the same deadpan-public-radio formula as the first joke but with a slightly lower ceiling — 'spoken-word opera about pear-shaped women' is funny for its specificity and sincerity but doesn't quite match the political audacity of the opener. Still very well-crafted absurdist writing.

dialogue.speaker: Derry Murbles
dialogue.line: I'm just a substitute host filling in for the regular guy who does this. I don't know what's going on half the time, but I show up, I do my job, and I go home.

dialogue.speaker: Derry Murbles
dialogue.line: Last week, they had me introduce something called 'The Pawnee Shoe Ballet' — it's exactly what it sounds like. Forty-seven minutes of people in leotards dancing while wearing different shoes. One guy did a interpretive dance about a Crocs sandal. A Crocs sandal! And the crowd gave him a standing ovation.

jokes.text: Leslie says she's 'here to send out the Bat-Signal,' and Derry responds by explaining to listeners what the Bat-Signal is, referring to 'the children's character the Bat-Man, a strong gentleman who fights crime nocturnally.'
jokes.setup: Leslie uses the colloquial phrase 'Bat-Signal' as a metaphor. Derry, in classic public-radio host fashion, clarifies for the audience.
jokes.punchline: Derry's earnest, archaic, technically accurate but socially oblivious description of Batman as 'the children's character the Bat-Man, a strong gentleman who fights crime nocturnally' is perfectly absurd over-explanation.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. 'A strong gentleman who fights crime nocturnally' is the funniest possible deadpan description of Batman — it's technically accurate, achingly formal, and reveals everything about Derry's voice. Leslie's 'That's correct. Well put.' completes it perfectly. Highly quotable and the best joke of the radio segment. Justifiably scores 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know, I just want to say that what you do here is really important. Radio is a vital medium, and you're doing great work.

dialogue.speaker: Radio Host
dialogue.line: Well, thank you. That's very kind of you to say.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I mean it. I was listening to your show on the way over here. You were doing a segment called 'Guess the Smell' where callers tried to identify odors you were describing over the phone.

dialogue.speaker: Radio Host
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's one of our most popular segments.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And it was fantastic. Really, really fantastic. Radio at its finest.

jokes.text: Leslie's increasingly desperate plea to listeners: 'send in your plan or your resume... And quick. Please. Hurry. This is all gonna fall apart if you don't hurry.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving a measured, professional pitch for public park design input on a radio show.
jokes.punchline: Her composure breaks into barely concealed panic — 'This is all gonna fall apart if you don't hurry' — revealing her anxiety underneath the professional veneer.
jokes.explanation: Deeply Leslie Knope — the crack in her professionalism revealing frantic energy underneath is perfect character comedy. The escalating 'quick... please... hurry... this is all gonna fall apart' is well-structured. High character integration score because only Leslie would break like this on live radio while trying to maintain composure.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: It's like Batman!

dialogue.speaker: Derry Murbles
dialogue.line: Batman is a 1960s television program about a man in a cape who fights crime in Gotham City. He is accompanied by a young ward named Robin. The show aired for three seasons on ABC and was notable for its campy tone and colorful villains such as the Riddler, the Penguin, and Catwoman. Batman's real identity is Bruce Wayne, a wealthy businessman who witnessed his parents' murder as a child, which motivated him to fight crime. He is equipped with various gadgets stored in his utility belt, including batarangs, a grappling hook, and shark repellent bat spray. His vehicle is called the Batmobile.

jokes.text: The radio show transitions to 'Jazz Plus Jazz Equals Jazz,' described as 'a recording of Benny Goodman played over a separate recording of Miles Davis.'
jokes.setup: Standard public-radio segment transition, announced earnestly.
jokes.punchline: The segment concept — two separate jazz recordings played simultaneously — presented as a legitimate programming choice, followed by the deadpan rationale 'Research shows that our listeners love jazz.'
jokes.explanation: The concept of 'jazz plus jazz equals jazz' as a programming philosophy is clever absurdism. The follow-up tag 'Research shows our listeners love jazz' in a separate talking-head beat punctuates it perfectly — implying the logic is airtight while being completely circular. Good economy and absurdist construction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to level with you. I need your help with the park design. I've tried everything - I've called every contractor, every engineer, every landscape architect in this city. And nobody will return my calls because apparently I have a 'reputation' for being 'difficult' and 'calling at 3 AM to discuss municipal code.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So I'm begging you. Please. I will do anything. I will name a park bench after you. I will name a entire section after you. I will name my firstborn child after you if you just help me with this one thing.

jokes.text: Leslie reads a park design submission that ends with: 'Also, I'm innocent. Please find me a lawyer.' — from a federal penitentiary.
jokes.setup: Leslie and her team are going through park design submissions, reading from letters.
jokes.punchline: The letter is from a federal penitentiary and tacks on a plea for legal help at the end of an otherwise earnest design submission.
jokes.explanation: Clean setup/punchline with good economy. The joke works because the prisoner treats the park design contest as a legitimate venue for a legal Hail Mary. 'Also, I'm innocent. Please find me a lawyer.' lands because of the casual 'also' — structuring a desperate plea as an afterthought.

jokes.text: Leslie describes Wreston's portfolio as 'Parks Department porn.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been describing Wreston's beautiful designs — fountain, manicured shrubbery.
jokes.punchline: She summarizes her visceral enthusiasm with the phrase 'This is like Parks Department porn,' perfectly capturing her over-the-top passion for civic planning.
jokes.explanation: High character integration because this line could only come from Leslie — her passion for parks is so extreme that 'porn' is the natural analogy. Maximum economy. The joke is earned because we've watched her rave about the design sincerely for two sentences. Highly quotable and captures the Leslie Knope essence efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Welcome to Radio Pawnee's Jazz After Dark. I'm your host, Leslie Knope. Tonight we're doing something revolutionary. We're going to play two jazz recordings at the same time.

dialogue.speaker: Radio Host
dialogue.line: That's just... that's just noise.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's what they said about bebop.

jokes.text: Leslie says 'I don't care if he's some junkie war criminal pimp. I am not gonna change my mind.' — then immediately reverses when she learns he's from Eagleton.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just declared with absolute conviction that nothing could change her mind about hiring Wreston.
jokes.punchline: Hearing he's from Eagleton instantly reverses her position — 'Oh, I've changed my mind' — with the same flat certainty she used to declare she wouldn't change her mind.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect joke structure. 'I don't care if he's some junkie war criminal pimp, I am not gonna change my mind' is an escalating hyperbolic oath that sets up the reversal. The punchline ('Oh, I've changed my mind') uses the exact same deadpan delivery as the oath, making the contrast hilarious. Also reveals Leslie's Eagleton prejudice as a character trait more extreme than any actual crime. Justifies the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Prison letter writer
dialogue.line: Dear Parks Department, I have some excellent ideas for your new park design. First, I suggest a perimeter fence at least 12 feet high with barbed wire. Second, watchtowers at each corner with armed guards. Third, a central recreation yard surrounded by cells. Also, if anyone asks, I never wrote this letter. And one more thing — do you know a good lawyer?

jokes.text: Leslie's anti-Eagleton rant: 'they would most likely exterminate everyone who isn't from Eagleton if they weren't so busy being obsessed with themselves.'
jokes.setup: Leslie begins explaining why she distrusts people from Eagleton.
jokes.punchline: Her grievances escalate to genocide-level accusations, deflated by the qualifier that they're too self-absorbed to follow through.
jokes.explanation: The escalation to 'exterminate' is bold and funny, and the qualifier 'if they weren't so busy being obsessed with themselves' perfectly undercuts it. Good character integration — Leslie's civic passion metastasizing into irrational tribalism is a rich vein the show mines well.

jokes.text: Leslie adds: 'God, that was close. Sometimes when I rant about Eagleton, I forget to breathe, and I pass out.'
jokes.setup: Leslie just finished a passionate rant about Eagleton.
jokes.punchline: She reveals that her Eagleton rants are so intense they physically incapacitate her — she passes out from not breathing.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy — her hatred is so consuming it literally stops her breathing. The casual 'God, that was close' frames it as routine. Strong character integration score because this level of pathological civic rivalry is uniquely Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm willing to work with anyone. Murderers, arsonists, people who talk in movie theaters...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't care. If you want to help me make Pawnee better, I will work with you.

jokes.text: Tom introduces the future location of Rent-A-Swag to his colleagues: 'Friends, former lovers, acquaintances, Jerry'
jokes.setup: Tom is about to make an exciting announcement about his new business venture to his colleagues.
jokes.punchline: His warm address escalates from 'friends' to 'former lovers' (bizarre overshare) and then the list bottoms out with 'acquaintances, Jerry' — Jerry's name delivered as a category below acquaintance.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and structure. The list escalates (friends → former lovers → acquaintances) in the expected way, then the final beat — 'Jerry' as his own separate diminished category — lands as a precision strike on the show's running Jerry-dismissal gag. The 'former lovers' is also a funny overshare. This joke does three things in eight words. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't care if he's the most talented designer in the world. I will not change my mind about this.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: He's from Eagleton.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're hiring him immediately.

jokes.text: Tom explains Rent-A-Swag: 'I started a business where I rent my fancy clothes to teens so their parents don't have to buy them nice things they'll just grow out of. So if you see a 14-year-old kid wearing a Louis Vuitton cravat, you know who to thank. Me. And Louis Vuitton for making some dope-ass cravats.'
jokes.setup: Tom pitches his new business concept.
jokes.punchline: The concept itself is absurd (renting luxury clothes to teenagers), then Tom adds 'Me. And Louis Vuitton for making some dope-ass cravats' — an earnest acknowledgment that shares credit with a luxury brand for making 'dope-ass' products.
jokes.explanation: Pure Tom Haverford character comedy — only Tom would open a luxury clothes rental for teenagers and cite Louis Vuitton cravats as a key product category. The pivot to crediting Louis Vuitton is a funny anti-climax that reveals his genuine fashion reverence. 'Dope-ass cravats' is a great juxtaposition of register.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not being melodramatic.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But if we don't pass this bill, it will be basically like genocide. It's literally genocide. Genocide.

jokes.text: Ron surveys the chaotic store interior and says 'Son, I love wildlife, but is a store the best place for it?' and we hear a 'Help.' from somewhere in the store.
jokes.setup: Tom has just introduced everyone to his new business location, implicitly showing off the space.
jokes.punchline: The store is apparently in such disarray that there is wildlife (implied animal) inside it, and someone (a mannequin? a person?) is crying for help.
jokes.explanation: A strong visual-gag/reaction-beat combo. Ron's deadpan question about wildlife is perfectly in character, and the disembodied 'Help.' — which we can't see the source of — escalates the chaos comedically. The follow-up 'Help. I can't move.' at 04:27 confirms it's a running gag. Ron's delivery as a man calmly observing a disaster is ideal character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Eagleton is the worst. Everything about it is the worst. The people, the parks, the government—it's all terrible. They think they're so much better than us, but they're not. They're arrogant and smug and I hate everything about that town.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I've actually thrown up from rage about Eagleton.

jokes.text: 'Much like women in '90s stand-up comedy routines, Tommy be shopping.'
jokes.setup: Tom reveals he has been spending lavishly on fancy clothes that form the inventory for his new business
jokes.punchline: He frames his shopping habit with a self-aware reference to a tired comedy cliché ('women love to shop'), but the grammar 'Tommy be shopping' also has a comedic flavor of its own
jokes.explanation: Clever meta-joke that simultaneously uses and pokes fun at a shopworn stereotype. Tom's pop-culture fluency and self-awareness are perfectly captured here. The meta-commentary on '90s stand-up is unexpectedly sharp for what's essentially a throwaway line. 'Tommy be shopping' as a comedic self-description has a nice rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jerry is so far below acquaintances on my social pyramid that he doesn't even have a tier. He's just... dirt. He's beneath dirt. He's the thing dirt looks down on.

jokes.text: Tom pitches the store's advantages: 'Good use of the word fiscal, Tommy -- very upscale. Very impressive. Watching you gives me faith that anyone can reinvent themselves.'
jokes.setup: Tom is listing the store's merits, including 'it's well within my fiscal range.'
jokes.punchline: Ann's praise of Tom for correctly using the word 'fiscal' — treating vocabulary as a significant accomplishment — is backhanded condescension disguised as encouragement. 'Anyone can reinvent themselves' implies the bar was very low.
jokes.explanation: Well-structured mild irony from Ann — the praise reads as genuine on the surface but 'watching you gives me faith that anyone can reinvent themselves' is a politely devastating comment. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I know what you're thinking. 'Tom, this is just the same tired business idea we've seen a thousand times.' And you're right. But that's exactly why it's going to work. I'm leaning into the cliché. It's meta. It's self-aware. It's... actually just a bad idea, isn't it?

jokes.text: Tom's talking-head: 'Tommy Timberlake is dead. Long live Thomas M. Haverford, responsible tycoon.'
jokes.setup: Tom is explaining his new business persona and his intention to be more responsible.
jokes.punchline: 'Tommy Timberlake' (a Justin Timberlake-referencing alter ego) is being officially retired, replaced by 'Thomas M. Haverford, responsible tycoon' — a title that is self-evidently grandiose for a man who currently has a crumbling store.
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable character comedy. 'Tommy Timberlake' is a great throwaway detail (Tom's self-styled celebrity alter ego), and 'responsible tycoon' is a perfectly contradictory self-description — 'tycoon' undermining the 'responsible' qualifier. Regal phrasing ('Long live') applied to a guy opening a teen clothing rental shop.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I want to thank everyone who helped me get here. My beautiful wife Donna, my best friend Jerry - I mean Larry - I mean Garry - anyway, my business partners, my mentors, and most importantly, my stylist.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Because let me tell you something - you can't achieve success in this world unless you're dressed to the nines in a Tom Ford suit with some fly kicks and a fresh fade. It's called high-low fashion, baby. That's Prada on top, Adidas on the bottom. That's how we do it in the Treat Yo' Self era.

jokes.text: Disembodied voice from inside the chaotic store: 'Help. I can't move.'
jokes.setup: Ron already noted wildlife in the store and heard 'Help' earlier. The store was described as needing work.
jokes.punchline: Now a more urgent, complete distress call — 'Help. I can't move.' — still unanswered and unaddressed by anyone, as the scene continues.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from the earlier 'Help.' to 'Help. I can't move.' — still completely ignored — is funny through pure absurdist commitment. Maximum economy (four words). The running gag pays off with greater urgency and greater indifference from the cast.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Help! Help! Can anybody hear me? I'm trapped under the table!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Is anyone going to help Jerry?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Please! Someone! Anything!

jokes.text: Ben walks into Wreston's current park and immediately complains: 'He designed this place? What a dump. There's no trash cans anywhere. What am I supposed to do with my garbage, just throw it on the ground?' — to which a nearby person says 'Oh, hey, thank you for the trash!'
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie have come to meet Wreston at his impressive existing park — Leslie is already impressed. Ben criticizes the park in real time.
jokes.punchline: Ben complains about no trash cans and rhetorically asks if he should just throw garbage on the ground. Someone near him instantly accepts his garbage, revealing the park is so pristine that a park-goer is happy to manage it — making Ben's complaint both petty and culturally telling.
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke — Ben's hyperbolic rhetorical complaint is immediately literalized by the park-goer cheerfully accepting the trash. It simultaneously satirizes Eagleton's over-manicured culture and deflates Ben's grumbling. Good setup/punchline construction with an unexpected third element.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'm still stuck! And now my leg is falling asleep!

jokes.text: Wreston's park is officially called 'Five Mile Grounds,' but locals call it 'Wide smiles abound.' Leslie asks 'Because of all the smiles that occur?' and Ben deadpans 'It's so boring.'
jokes.setup: Wreston proudly shares the park's nickname and its meaning.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's literal follow-up ('Because of all the smiles that occur?') is sweet and slightly dim. Ben's flat 'It's so boring' cuts through both the nickname and the general niceness of the place.
jokes.explanation: Ben's deadpan 'It's so boring' is well-timed and reveals his cultural skepticism toward Eagleton niceness. Leslie's oblivious follow-up question adds a layer. Good economy and character work.

dialogue.speaker: Wreston
dialogue.line: Of course, feel free to just throw your garbage anywhere. That's what Pawnee does best.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh, thank you!

dialogue.speaker: Wreston
dialogue.line: No, I was being sarcastic.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Too late, I already threw it.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head: 'He seems super-cool.' followed immediately by Ben's: 'He seems cool. Just you wait.' — then cut back to the park tour.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben give competing assessments of Wreston in talking-heads.
jokes.punchline: Ben's ominous 'Just you wait' positions his skepticism of Eagleton as the wiser view — ironic given that Leslie's prejudice (not his) turns out to be the issue.
jokes.explanation: A competent talking-head juxtaposition joke. Ben's dramatic 'just you wait' is mildly funny given his tone, but the joke is fairly standard for the format. Works as character contrast.

dialogue.speaker: Pawnee citizen
dialogue.line: There are no trash cans in this park!

dialogue.speaker: Pawnee citizen
dialogue.line: I have to carry my garbage around like some kind of pack mule.

dialogue.speaker: Pawnee citizen
dialogue.line: Wait... I just realized something. Having to hold onto my garbage all day has made me grateful for it. My trash is a part of me now.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head about Eagletonians: 'Well, they always wine and dine you first, but the fact of the matter is Eagletonians are, without exception, snobby, condescending jerks.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben just had a pleasant experience with Wreston at the park.
jokes.punchline: Leslie interprets the pleasant experience as a deliberate manipulation tactic ('they always wine and dine you first'), unable to update her priors despite evidence.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Leslie's bias is so total that genuine kindness reads as predatory strategy. 'They always wine and dine you first' reframes hospitality as threat. Consistent with her established characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Preston
dialogue.line: Welcome to Pawnee's newest park, brought to you by the generous donation from our neighbors in Eagleton.

dialogue.speaker: Preston
dialogue.line: We're calling it... Eagleton Commons.

dialogue.speaker: Eagleton Representative
dialogue.line: Actually, we prefer 'Eagleton Commons' — with the accent on the second syllable. It's French.

jokes.text: Visual gag: The camera shows the contrast between the Pawnee side of the border and the Eagleton side — audience audibly reacts 'Ah. Uhh.' as the beautiful/terrible contrast is revealed.
jokes.setup: Wreston is giving the tour and mentions 'this is the Pawnee side of our border with Eagleton... and this is the Eagleton side.'
jokes.punchline: The visual contrast between the two sides is apparently so stark it prompts an involuntary vocal reaction from Leslie and Ben — the joke is entirely in the implied image and the characters' helpless acknowledgment of Eagleton's superiority.
jokes.explanation: A strong visual gag that lands entirely on contrast. The transcript's 'Ah. Uhh.' represents characters seeing the difference and being speechless — a reaction beat that implies the visual punchline. Maximum economy in the transcript. Rewatch value because the actual visual is presumably devastating.

dialogue.line: Stark visual contrast showing inequality between the two towns at the border

jokes.text: April calls Ben at City Hall and asks to 'come down here and keep me company.' April's condition: 'If I come down there, can I at least break something?' Ben: 'Of course, baby. Anything. You know that.'
jokes.setup: April calls Ben at the boring security guard post, asking to visit.
jokes.punchline: April's request to be allowed to break something as a condition of visiting, and Ben's completely casual acceptance ('Of course, baby. Anything. You know that'), frames casual destruction as a normal part of their relationship.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character integration — April's need to destroy something to alleviate boredom, and Andy's total unsurprised acceptance ('You know that'), reveals their relationship dynamic perfectly. The 'Of course, baby. Anything. You know that' is especially good — the 'you know that' implies this is an established pattern. Justifies 8+ through pure character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey, does anyone want to hang out with me while I'm on security guard duty? I'm gonna be here all night and it's really lonely.

jokes.text: Andy's talking-head about the security guard job: 'I did everything I was supposed to do, and I walked around the building four times. Only 20 minutes has gone by. Ugh! Thought maybe ten minutes had gone by since I started talking. It's only been 15 seconds. Ohh...'
jokes.setup: Andy is explaining that the security guard job is boring.
jokes.punchline: His boredom is so profound that even talking about time passing doesn't pass time — his self-pity escalates to checking how long he's been talking, only to find 15 seconds elapsed. The 'Ohh...' is a perfect deflated reaction.
jokes.explanation: Smart structural escalation — Andy's complaint about time not passing becomes meta when the confession itself fails to pass time. The '15 seconds' reveal is a well-timed punchline within the talking-head format. Andy's particular brand of simple, genuine despair is perfectly captured.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've been a security guard for 20 minutes and I've already done so much. I've walked around, I've looked at things, I've... I've written down some numbers.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, what numbers did I write down?

jokes.text: April arrives and Andy says: 'Oh, babe, thank God you're here. I got so bored, I started thinking about existence — do I matter? Do any of us? Is there a master plan in the works, a grand design? Just dumb stuff like that.' April: 'Ugh! Who cares?'
jokes.setup: Andy was so bored he fell into existential contemplation. April arrives and he describes his philosophical musings.
jokes.punchline: Andy's existential spiral (do I matter? is there a grand design?) is immediately dismissed by himself as 'Just dumb stuff like that,' and April's response — 'Ugh! Who cares?' — validates his self-dismissal with perfect nihilist impatience.
jokes.explanation: Two-tier joke. Andy's self-dismissal of his own existential crisis ('just dumb stuff like that') is sweet and character-perfect. April's 'Ugh! Who cares?' is both funny in isolation and a perfect April-ism that defines her character in three words. Together they form an ideal Andy-April comedic beat. High character integration for both. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm bored. I need to do something.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, what am I doing? Why am I here? What's the point of anything?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh God, I'm having an existential crisis. This is bad. This is really bad.

jokes.text: Andy wonders aloud: 'Wait a minute. Isn't this how all great Bert Macklin cases start? [pause] It's quiet. A little too quiet.'
jokes.setup: Andy has been lamenting the boredom of security guard duty.
jokes.punchline: He reframes the boredom as the setup for a Bert Macklin FBI adventure — his fictional secret agent alter ego — and delivers 'It's quiet. A little too quiet' as a dramatic beat that is simultaneously a cliché and earnestly committed.
jokes.explanation: The Bert Macklin character is beloved, and this transition from bored security guard to FBI agent mindset is a perfect Andy beat. 'It's quiet. A little too quiet.' is a cliché, but Andy's sincere delivery of it makes it funny rather than hacky. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: What if we're all just living in a simulation?

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Then I hope it crashes.

jokes.text: Wreston mentions the 'massive sewage overflow in Circle Park' casually. Leslie says 'We totally fixed it.' Ben adds: 'Well, except for the smell. The scientists think it's going to linger for another 40 years.'
jokes.setup: Wreston brings up a past embarrassment for Pawnee in the middle of what is supposed to be a positive tour.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's defensive 'We totally fixed it' is immediately contradicted by Ben's calm, factual qualification that the smell will last 40 years — undermining Leslie's claim while sounding even more alarming.
jokes.explanation: Good comedy of deflation. Ben's calm, specific '40 years' makes the joke land — it's precise enough to sound credible, devastating enough to be funny. Leslie's defensive overstatement followed by Ben's matter-of-fact contradiction is a reliable comedic structure used well here.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: This security job is so boring. I'm just standing here watching monitors all day.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm not Andy Dwyer, security guard. I'm Detective Slash Speedchaser, private investigator on the case of the Missing Donuts.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The trail is cold, but Slash Speedchaser never gives up.

jokes.text: Leslie compares herself to 'a Southern belle when Rhett Butler comes around' re: Wreston. Leslie agrees: 'Yes. Rhett Butler. That's who he reminds me of. Or Bono!' Ben: 'What?'
jokes.setup: Ben teases Leslie about being charmed by Wreston despite her stated prejudice.
jokes.punchline: Leslie accepts the Rhett Butler comparison earnestly and then, apparently in the same mental motion, adds 'Or Bono!' — an utterly incongruous addition that Ben can only respond to with 'What?'
jokes.explanation: The 'Or Bono!' non sequitur is perfectly Leslie — the two names share nothing except, apparently, some quality only she perceives. Ben's 'What?' is exactly the right reaction and exactly the right length of response. The joke works through Leslie's specific brand of earnest, scrambled enthusiasm.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The dame walked in, and I knew right away she was trouble. She had legs that went all the way up to her... legs.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'd been a detective for fifteen years, and I'd never seen anything like it. Well, except for that one time. And that other time.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: She said, 'Bert Macklin, I need your help.' I said, 'Lady, I help everyone. It's what I do.'

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head: 'In 1988, we were hit by a tornado. We asked Eagleton for help, and they claimed they weren't home. An entire town claimed they weren't home.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining why she distrusts Eagleton, citing a historical grievance.
jokes.punchline: The grievance — that the entire town of Eagleton collectively pretended not to be home when Pawnee called for disaster relief — is absurdist in its specificity and scale. The repetition 'An entire town claimed they weren't home' underlines it perfectly.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'An entire town claimed they weren't home' is absurdist genius — applying the most mundane social excuse (not answering the door) to an entire municipality in response to a disaster. The repetition for emphasis shows confident comic writing. High marks across all dimensions. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, the sewage overflow is finally fixed.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Only took thirty years and a class action lawsuit.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: At least it's done now.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Done? Ben, we're still finding fish with three eyes in the Wamapoke River.

jokes.text: Wreston has commissioned a balloon portrait of Leslie and Ben from the balloon artisan — Leslie and Ben look at a balloon version of themselves.
jokes.setup: Wreston left briefly to tend to the balloon artisan. Leslie is skeptical; Ben is charmed.
jokes.punchline: Wreston returns with balloon portraits of Leslie and Ben as a gesture of good will — a comically elaborate, totally sincere gift that visually deflates Leslie's suspicions.
jokes.explanation: A good visual gag — the balloon artisan detail was established earlier, and the callback of commissioning personalized balloon portraits of the visiting skeptics is a sweet, slightly absurd gesture. Works better as a visual than as a transcript joke, hence slightly lower scores, but the rewatch value is high.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Eagleton is so selfish, they literally pretended the entire town wasn't home when we tried to visit.

jokes.text: Tom's talking-head on Rent-A-Swag as business philosophy: 'Rent-A-Swag is gonna be the opposite of Entertainment720. This is my last chance. If this goes down in flames, I will have nothing except my looks. I could always pimp myself out to hot older ladies. I need to remember that.'
jokes.setup: Tom is describing the stakes of Rent-A-Swag.
jokes.punchline: His contingency plan — pimping himself to 'hot older ladies' — is delivered as a genuine comfort thought, followed by the earnest self-reminder 'I need to remember that,' as though filing it as actionable backup.
jokes.explanation: Tom's contingency plan is character-perfect — 'I need to remember that' treats gigolo-dom as a serious, viable backup that he simply doesn't want to forget. Only Tom would take legitimate comfort in this and find it reassuring enough to actively note for future reference.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, is that... is that supposed to be me?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A balloon artist made sculptures of us! Isn't it amazing?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It looks like I'm having a stroke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's just the balloon artist's style.

jokes.text: Tom greets Jerry: 'Jerry! How's the old ticker?' Jerry starts to answer, Tom immediately moves on: 'Great! Glad to hear it.'
jokes.setup: Tom is performing the Iacocca 'small connection' management technique on his team
jokes.punchline: When he gets to Jerry, he asks about his heart (Jerry is recovering from a heart attack) but cuts off his answer immediately, having satisfied himself that he asked
jokes.explanation: Excellent Jerry joke. The structure is tight — the setup (Iacocca technique) makes the dismissal of Jerry's actual answer funnier, because Tom literally just read that he should connect with workers, and still can't bring himself to hear Jerry out. Economy is near-perfect. The 'old ticker' after Jerry's actual heart health issue adds a dark specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm trying this new management style where I compliment my employees on their work ethic and appearance.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That sounds inappropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, no, it's great. Like, 'Jerry, you filed those forms perfectly, and those khakis really bring out your eyes.'

jokes.text: Leslie's historical mini-lecture: 'May, 1817. A scrappy group of frontiersmen and women arrive at a hardscrabble chunk of land and call it Pawnee, Indiana.' / 'June, 1817, the richest among them take all of their money from the bank and then flee up the hill like cowards to form Eagleton.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining the historical origins of the Pawnee-Eagleton rivalry to Wreston.
jokes.punchline: The history is presented in the cadence of a solemn civic lesson, but June 1817 — one month later — they 'flee up the hill like cowards.' The timeline compression (one month gap between founding and betrayal) and the editorial 'like cowards' are the comedy.
jokes.explanation: Leslie narrating history with her own editorial slant ('like cowards') is perfect character comedy. The one-month gap between Pawnee's founding and Eagleton's formation from fleeing rich people is a satisfying absurd detail. Her solemn cadence applied to petty grudge-keeping is consistently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So Jerry, how are you feeling these days?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, I've been having some back pain and—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's great! Glad to hear you're doing so well.

jokes.text: Wreston points out he has ancestors on both sides of the Pawnee-Eagleton divide and calls the rivalry 'just a little silly and self-defeating.' Ben drops: 'You may not know this, but Leslie was actually born in Eagleton.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just delivered an impassioned history of the evil of Eagleton.
jokes.punchline: Ben reveals that Leslie herself was born in Eagleton — the ultimate irony that deflates her entire prejudicial position.
jokes.explanation: A well-deployed irony bomb. Ben's casual 'You may not know this' makes the reveal feel even more pointed — it's information he's been sitting on while Leslie rants. Leslie's response 'Do not blame me for the sins of my mother' is also very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: In 1817, Pawnee was founded by a group of brave pioneers who wanted to build a community based on hard work, integrity, and American values. Eagleton, on the other hand, was founded by cowards who were too afraid to stay in Pawnee.

jokes.text: Leslie's response to being outed as Eagleton-born: 'Do not blame me for the sins of my mother.'
jokes.setup: Ben has just revealed Leslie was born in Eagleton.
jokes.punchline: Leslie deflects with a quasi-religious formulation — 'do not blame me for the sins of my mother' — treating her birthplace as a moral failing requiring theological absolution.
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable. The biblical phrasing ('sins of my mother') applied to the mundane fact of one's birthplace is perfect Leslie Knope comedy — grandiose register for a petty civic rivalry. Maximum economy. Strong originality in the framing. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie was born in Eagleton.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No! That's... that's my original sin!

jokes.text: Leslie, to Wreston who is considering leaving: 'Oh... running away so soon. Typical.' / 'You know, say what you want about Pawneeans, but we never give up. We have a mural called The Many Surrenders of Pawnee.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to guilt Wreston into staying despite being rude to him. She invokes Pawneean resilience.
jokes.punchline: Her defense of Pawnee's never-give-up attitude is immediately undercut by the existence of a mural commemorating their many surrenders — the mural's name perfectly contradicting her point.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'We have a mural called The Many Surrenders of Pawnee' is peak Parks and Rec worldbuilding comedy — it implies a rich civic history of giving up, commemorated in art, cited by Leslie as she argues for Pawnee's resilience. The self-defeating irony is perfect. Highly quotable, great economy, strong originality. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Pawneeans never give up.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're made of stronger stuff than that.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, what does that mural say?

dialogue.speaker: Tour Guide
dialogue.line: Oh, that celebrates all the times Pawnee surrendered without fighting.

jokes.text: The Bert Macklin sequence: Andy interrogates April as 'Miss Hitler, spoiled only daughter of Adolf,' demanding the 'necklace with all of Germany's war secrets.'
jokes.setup: Andy has invented a Bert Macklin FBI roleplay scenario to stave off boredom. April participates as a character.
jokes.punchline: April's character is 'Judy Hitler, spoiled only daughter of Adolf' — an absurd villain premise that April commits to fully. The object of desire is 'the necklace with all of Germany's war secrets' — an escalatingly specific MacGuffin.
jokes.explanation: The Bert Macklin universe is a beloved recurring element of the show. The joke here is the commitment of both Andy and April to a completely insane fiction — April choosing 'Judy Hitler' without hesitation, the 'war secrets necklace' as a plot device, and April's escalation into full villainy. Pure character comedy that only works because of who these two people are.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So you're telling me you're Hitler's daughter?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's right. My mother was a deer.

jokes.text: Andy, playing Bert Macklin, interrogates someone: 'The name is special agent Bert Macklin. Tell me who you are, who you work for, and don't bother trying to lie to me, because I'm amazing.'
jokes.setup: Andy has fully shifted into Bert Macklin mode and is interrogating someone in City Hall.
jokes.punchline: 'Don't bother trying to lie to me, because I'm amazing' — the action-hero confidence qualifier is 'I'm amazing' rather than anything legitimately threatening.
jokes.explanation: A good Bert Macklin bit. The thriller-interrogation formula is correctly assembled ('tell me who you are, who you work for') and then punctured by the self-assessment 'because I'm amazing' — which is both entirely Andy and entirely Bert Macklin.

dialogue.speaker: Andy (as Bert Macklin)
dialogue.line: So you're telling me you have an inappropriate attraction to a fictional Hitler character?

dialogue.speaker: Andy (as Bert Macklin)
dialogue.line: That's... that's not good.

jokes.text: Andy threatens 'torture' and April/Judy Hitler immediately capitulates: 'Fine. I will show you where it is, damn it.'
jokes.setup: Andy/Bert Macklin has been threatening April/Judy Hitler in the interrogation.
jokes.punchline: Judy Hitler folds instantly at the mere mention of torture — maximum anti-climax in a spy thriller structure.
jokes.explanation: The immediate capitulation undercuts the spy thriller tension perfectly. April's 'Fine. I will show you where it is, damn it' is funny because she gives up both the MacGuffin and the character (the 'damn it' is April-frustration leaking through Judy Hitler).

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ron, I'm concerned about the wood grain direction. Does it affect structural integrity? Should I be using a different type of wood? What if the finish isn't food-safe? How do I know if my measurements are precise enough?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's a birdhouse, Chris.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Right, but what if the birds have ethical concerns about the adhesive I used?

jokes.text: Andy/Bert Macklin: 'You're too good, Macklin. Don't you dare fall in love with me.' / 'Oh, Hitler, you sexy bastard. No! Yes!' — followed by apparent makeout.
jokes.setup: The Bert Macklin interrogation has shifted into a spy-film romantic tension scene.
jokes.punchline: Andy plays BOTH sides of the cliché spy romance — warning himself not to fall in love, then succumbing — while April remains in character as Judy Hitler. The 'Oh, Hitler, you sexy bastard' is the peak absurdist moment.
jokes.explanation: The escalation to Andy voicing both roles in the spy romance while April remains committed to being Judy Hitler reaches true absurdist heights. 'Oh, Hitler, you sexy bastard. No! Yes!' is structurally a classic internal conflict monologue applied to an absurd situation — the payoff is the name 'Hitler' in a romantic context, which is audacious and lands through sheer commitment. Highly quotable. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I tried to fix the joint, but I think I actually made it worse.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I don't really know what I'm doing with woodworking.

jokes.text: Ann walks in on Andy and April apparently in some state of post-roleplay: 'I am just filled to the brim with questions.'
jokes.setup: Ann has walked in on the aftermath of the Bert Macklin/Judy Hitler scenario.
jokes.punchline: Ann's reaction 'I am just filled to the brim with questions' is a masterpiece of deliberate underreaction — she's clearly overwhelmed but chooses to process it with a remarkably composed statement.
jokes.explanation: Maximally economical reaction beat. 'I am just filled to the brim with questions' is a perfect line — 'filled to the brim' is such a specific, almost genteel phrasing for a moment of complete bewilderment. Ann's character as the show's reasonable straight-man reacting to chaos is perfectly deployed here. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm going to give you a woodworking project. It's pointless, it has no purpose, and when you're done, we're going to burn it.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ron, I don't think that's going to help.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude. Now grab a chisel.

jokes.text: Chris interrogates woodworking questions: 'Why are you using this wood? Is it more pliable? What are these metal latches? Are they copper or brass? Is one better? And if so, why?' Ron responds: 'If I tell you, then you won't have learned anything.'
jokes.setup: Chris is studying woodworking with Ron as part of therapy-recommended non-exercise hobbies.
jokes.punchline: Ron's response to a barrage of practical questions — 'If I tell you, then you won't have learned anything' — is a Zen-master deflection that sounds profound but is actually just Ron refusing to explain things.
jokes.explanation: Ron's pedagogical style — Socratic deflection as laziness — is perfectly captured. Chris's rapid-fire questions set up the deflation beautifully, and Ron's non-answer sounds wise while meaning nothing. 'Another in a long line of lessons from the great Ron Swanson' from Chris lands as earnest appreciation for a non-answer. Strong character integration for both.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Who does Wreston sound like?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: He sounds like a combination of a dictator and a fictional villain.

jokes.text: Chris's talking-head: 'My therapist, Dr. Richard Nygard, suggested that I try some non-exercise-based hobbies. So I've been studying woodworking with Ron. I made this.' [shows something] 'Before I started, it was bigger.'
jokes.setup: Chris is explaining his woodworking hobby with Ron.
jokes.punchline: 'Before I started, it was bigger' — Chris has apparently made his woodworking project smaller, implying he destroyed more wood than he built. The object (unseen) is presumably a disaster.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest lines. 'Before I started, it was bigger' is delivered earnestly as additional context, but it recontextualizes everything — he hasn't built anything, he's destroyed a block of wood. The implication is maximum with minimum words. Chris's cheerful delivery of this damning fact is perfect. Near-perfect economy score. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey, has anyone seen my Hitler impersonator? We were supposed to do a bit about park safety but he never showed up.

jokes.text: Ron hands Chris a design: 'Here. I have designed something very important. Why don't you start work on that right away?' — revealed to be 'a flight of stairs that leads to nowhere.'
jokes.setup: Ron is teaching Chris woodworking and gives him a design to build.
jokes.punchline: The important design is a staircase to nowhere — functionally useless, Zen-absurd, and exactly what Ron Swanson would find meaningful as an exercise.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Ron Swanson bit. The escalation from 'something very important' to 'a flight of stairs that leads to nowhere' is a great subversion — Ron genuinely believes in the value of the work itself regardless of destination, making this both absurdist and oddly in-character. Highly quotable. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I want to apologize for what I said. It was wrong and insensitive.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But in my defense, my prejudices are completely legitimate.

jokes.text: Ben tells Leslie that Wreston sounds just like her. Leslie's response: 'You know who he sounds like, right? Yes. Idi Amin. Or Lord Voldemort.'
jokes.setup: Ben is pointing out that Wreston's philosophy about serving the public mirrors Leslie's own values.
jokes.punchline: Leslie entirely misreads the cue and offers Idi Amin and Lord Voldemort as the referents — people who sound like her, per her bizarre logic.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Idi Amin' as the first guess is very funny — an East African dictator as the person Leslie feels sounds most like her. The list (a real dictator + a fictional villain) escalates well. Pure character comedy showing Leslie's bias distorting reality.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I just want to say I'm really sorry about what happened. I feel terrible and I want to make it right.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Leslie Knope, Deputy Director of the Parks Department.

jokes.text: Leslie begins her apology to Wreston and repeatedly fails to say 'sorry': 'I'm s... I'm sor... I'm sor-- He's a human being. You're a human being. You can just-- just say-- I'm sor-- I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry.'
jokes.setup: Ben has pressured Leslie into apologizing to Wreston. She has agreed in principle but is physically incapable of delivering the word.
jokes.punchline: Leslie cannot say 'sorry' — the word physically resists her. Ben coaches her out loud in front of Wreston while she stutters. The eventual 'I'm sorry' is delivered in a rush after agonizing buildup.
jokes.explanation: Extended cringe comedy at its best. The escalating failure to say 'sorry' is perfectly structured — each attempt ('I'm s...', 'I'm sor...') ratchets up the discomfort, Ben coaching mid-apology adds another layer, and Leslie's Canada Dry non sequitur ('My mouth is dry. This is Canada Dry. Drink Canada Dry if your mouth is dry.') is a surreal panic diversion. The apology itself, when it finally comes, is anti-climactically rapid after the enormous buildup. This is a standout sequence. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm really sorry, I shouldn't have said those things. I feel terrible and I want to make it up to you. That's why I got you this gift — a six-pack of refreshing Coca-Cola Zero Sugar, which has all the taste of regular Coke but with zero calories, zero sugar, and zero artificial sweeteners.

jokes.text: Mid-apology, Leslie says: 'My mouth is dry. This is Canada Dry. Drink Canada Dry if your mouth is dry. That's nothing. What I want to say is...'
jokes.setup: Leslie is stalling while trying to say 'sorry' and grabs a nearby beverage.
jokes.punchline: She reads the brand name aloud as a slogan, realizes it's irrelevant, and immediately self-corrects — 'That's nothing' — as if she almost got distracted into giving a Canada Dry commercial.
jokes.explanation: The best single joke in the episode. Leslie's brain, stalling for time, latches onto the Canada Dry logo and she begins advertising it — 'Drink Canada Dry if your mouth is dry' — then catches herself: 'That's nothing.' The moment captures peak panic Leslie. It's unexpected, character-specific, memorable, and the self-awareness ('that's nothing') is perfectly timed. 'What I want to say is...' then resumes the cringe. Highly quotable. Justifies the top score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm sorry. I'm so sorry. I'm really, really sorry.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I apologize. I sincerely apologize. I deeply and profoundly apologize.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Can you forgive me? Will you forgive me? Please forgive me?

jokes.text: After the apology finally lands, Wreston offers to design the park pro bono. Leslie responds: 'That's very nice of you. I've been working up a little model of the design— why don't I bring it over and we can all go through it together.' Leslie: 'Great. And then you can come to our wedding.' Wreston: 'Huh?' Ben: 'What?'
jokes.setup: A professional partnership is being established. Wreston offers a gesture of good faith.
jokes.punchline: Leslie spontaneously invites Wreston to their (unplanned) wedding — 'It's in May, and we haven't planned it yet, but save the date' — blindsiding both Wreston and Ben simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: The dual 'Huh?' / 'What?' reaction from Wreston and Ben simultaneously is a great comedy structure — Leslie has surprised both the stranger and her own fiancé equally. The detail 'It's in May, and we haven't planned it yet, but save the date' is perfectly Leslie — inviting someone to a wedding that doesn't exist yet with the confidence of a wedding planner. Wreston's 'I was never here' (escaping) is the cherry on top.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, we should invite you to our wedding!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, we just met him.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, but he's designing our park. That's basically family.

jokes.text: Wreston says 'I was never here' and flees the room. Cut to: 'Ah!'/'Aah!' — both Leslie and Ben startled as he apparently disappears.
jokes.setup: Wreston is apparently so flustered by the wedding invitation that he makes a quick exit.
jokes.punchline: His theatrical 'I was never here' followed by their startled exclamations implies a comedically abrupt departure.
jokes.explanation: A decent reaction beat. 'I was never here' is a funny line, and the startled exits from Leslie and Ben are implied to be funny visually. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: These mannequins look depressed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: They're not depressed, they're just realistic.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: No, they're depressed. Look at that one—she's given up on life.

jokes.text: Tom surveys Rent-A-Swag and describes the current decor issues: 'Do you really like this yellow paint? I mean, I know it was on sale, but it looks a lot like dried phlegm.' / 'I think one of the mannequins tried to commit suicide.'
jokes.setup: Tom is asking his friends for honest feedback on the store's current state.
jokes.punchline: Ann's critique — 'I think one of the mannequins tried to commit suicide' — is a darkly specific observation that paints the store's condition as so bleak that its inanimate occupants are despairing.
jokes.explanation: Both the 'dried phlegm' yellow paint description (specific and disgusting) and the suicidal mannequin line land well. The mannequin joke is the stronger of the two — dark, specific, and highly quotable. Tom's 'dried phlegm' shows good comedic instinct for gross-accurate color description.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Everyone, I'm throwing a pizza party! All the toppings are free.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Really? All free?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, cheese doesn't count as a topping.

jokes.text: Tom's store inspection: 'Do you really like this yellow paint? I know it was on sale, but it looks a lot like dried phlegm.' / 'I think one of the mannequins tried to commit suicide.'
jokes.setup: Tom is asking for honest feedback on his store renovation
jokes.punchline: The feedback is brutally specific — 'dried phlegm' and the suicide mannequin — delivered as matter-of-fact observations rather than hyperbole
jokes.explanation: Good feedback roast jokes. 'Dried phlegm' is a vivid, specific description that earns its laugh. The mannequin line (also referenced earlier) continues the dark theme. Functional, solid, not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not interested in joining your party. A party with no cake, no dancing, and no one I know sounds like my idea of a perfect evening.

jokes.text: Tom's 'pizza party' for his team: One small pizza for all of them. With no toppings. Tom: 'Cheese is a topping, Jerry.'
jokes.setup: Tom announces a 'pizza party' as a treat for the team's hard work.
jokes.punchline: The party is one small cheese-less pizza split among multiple people. When Jerry apparently objects to the lack of cheese, Tom clarifies with complete seriousness: 'Cheese is a topping, Jerry.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect setup/punchline. The 'pizza party' reveal — one small cheese-less pizza — escalates beautifully from the grandiose announcement. 'Cheese is a topping, Jerry' is a highly quotable line that works on two levels: Tom being genuinely cheap AND Tom correcting Jerry on cheese taxonomy. The specificity of having a pizza without cheese while calling it a pizza party is excellent. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey there, buddy. I'm Bert Macklin, FBI. I'm gonna need you to come with me.

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: I'm lost. I want my mom.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Your mom? That's exactly what a criminal would say. Now, we can do this the easy way or the hard way...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait. Wait, how old are you?

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: Six.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God, I am so sorry. I thought you were... I'm not actually FBI. I'm just a regular person who got really into this character. Your mom is probably really worried. Let me help you find her.

jokes.text: Ron's reaction to the pizza party: 'And why are these lights blaring, by the way? Does someone here own stock in the electric company?' / 'If there were more food and fewer people, this would be a perfect party.'
jokes.setup: Ron is attending Tom's extremely meager pizza party.
jokes.punchline: Ron's ideal party conditions — 'more food and fewer people' — is a precise encapsulation of his anti-social, food-prioritizing worldview. His complaint about the lights is also a perfect Ron-ism.
jokes.explanation: 'If there were more food and fewer people, this would be a perfect party' is an all-time Ron Swanson line. It's both a devastating party review and a precise philosophical statement about his relationship with social interaction. Near-perfect character integration and economy. Highly quotable in any context. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Eagleton architect
dialogue.line: We've designed this park with Pawnee's unique demographic in mind. Notice the extra-wide benches and reinforced railings.

dialogue.speaker: Eagleton architect
dialogue.line: We also included drainage systems throughout, for the... drooling.

jokes.text: Ron: 'If there were more food and fewer people, this would be a perfect party.'
jokes.setup: Ron surveys Tom's cheese-free, one-pizza 'pizza party'
jokes.punchline: Ron's critique encompasses both the insufficient food AND the presence of people — he'd prefer a party with more of the former and none of the latter
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Ron jokes and one of its most quotable lines. Perfect economy — the sentence does two things simultaneously: criticizes the food quantity AND dismisses the guests as a negative variable. 'Fewer people' is the key beat; Ron is technically at a party and would prefer no other humans. High character integration — this is pure, concentrated Ron Swanson worldview in one sentence. Comparable in quality to classic Ron one-liners from across the series.

dialogue.speaker: Eagleton architect
dialogue.line: Your park design is fundamentally flawed. The pathways don't follow proper feng shui principles.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Feng shui? It's a public park, not a meditation temple.

dialogue.speaker: Eagleton architect
dialogue.line: Exactly. Which is why we need to install separate water fountains for the common folk. They're like animals — they need to be herded.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Did he really just compare us to livestock?

dialogue.speaker: Eagleton architect
dialogue.line: Not just herded. Caged. We should fence off the park into designated zones by income level.

jokes.text: The Bert Macklin escalation: Andy, still in character, stops a young boy exploring: 'A child spy, sent to steal the necklace? Bert Macklin, FBI! Freeze!'
jokes.setup: Andy is in Bert Macklin mode following the earlier roleplay. An actual child wanders into his sphere.
jokes.punchline: Andy applies the Bert Macklin fiction to a real child, terrifying him — the stakes of the roleplay escalating into actual child-frightening.
jokes.explanation: The Bert Macklin fiction colliding with an actual civilian child is a natural escalation of the running gag. April's immediate 'Yeah, bad call, Bert' is a great reality-check that implies she's been maintaining the fiction until it became a genuine problem.

dialogue.speaker: Eagleton architect
dialogue.line: Your park is small. Eagleton's parks are twice the size of yours.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Our park may be smaller, but it's efficient. We don't waste money on unnecessary amenities like you do.

dialogue.speaker: Eagleton architect
dialogue.line: Efficient? You call that pile of dirt efficient? In Eagleton, we have parks with water features, sculpture gardens, and proper landscaping.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Well, maybe your parks are bigger, but Pawnee's park has heart.

dialogue.speaker: Eagleton architect
dialogue.line: Heart? How quaint. Though I suppose when your park is the size of a postage stamp, heart is all you have room for.

jokes.text: Andy breaks character and tells the lost child: 'Oh, hey, I'm just kidding, buddy. I'm just playing around. My name's really Andy Dwyer. I'm a security guard... I've gotten lost here about 500 times, and I work here.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just terrified a small boy and needs to de-escalate.
jokes.punchline: Andy's reassurance includes 'I've gotten lost here about 500 times, and I work here' — meant to be comforting but implying Andy is also chronically confused and incompetent as a security guard.
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Andy's attempt to comfort a child inadvertently reveals his own incompetence. 'I've gotten lost here about 500 times' as a reassurance is perfectly Andy: he intends it as solidarity but it implies he's terrible at his job.

jokes.text: Wreston's employees present a park model that includes 'drool buckets for your more... slack-jawed citizens,' 'food troughs full of cheeseburgers,' and 'public showers with instructions for those who've never showered before.'
jokes.setup: Wreston's team comes to present their park design to the Pawnee parks department.
jokes.punchline: The design assumes Pawneeans are subhuman — complete with drool buckets, food troughs, and illustrated shower instructions — the most condescending possible interpretation of 'serving the public.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy that validates Leslie's Eagleton paranoia at the worst possible moment — right after she's been working hard to overcome her prejudice. The escalating specificity (drool buckets → food troughs → shower instructions) is well-constructed. 'Drool buckets for your more... slack-jawed citizens' is the peak, with the pause before 'slack-jawed' being the tell. Strong originality and structure. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so here's what we're going to do. First, we'll key their car. Then we'll put a dead fish in their air vents. Then we'll set their house on fire.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Leslie, no arson!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Fine. But I'm doing the fish thing.

jokes.text: Leslie's response to the presentation: 'You have five seconds to get out of here... Or I will rip your throats out. Out. Now.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just been presented with the insulting park model.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's usually diplomatic public servant persona shatters into 'I will rip your throats out' — the violence of the response contrasted with her normal comportment.
jokes.explanation: The violence of Leslie's reaction is funny for its contrast with her personality. 'I will rip your throats out' (plural — both of them) followed by 'Out. Now.' as crisp command is good comedic compression. The escalation from five-second warning to throat-ripping is solid.

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: Thank you so much for saving me!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You're welcome, buddy!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, we're just happy you're safe.

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: Thank you, Hitler!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa—what did you just call me?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I think he said 'Hitler.'

jokes.text: One of Wreston's employees, on the way out: 'Oh, hey, my backyard is bigger than your park.'
jokes.setup: The employees are being expelled from the meeting after their insulting presentation.
jokes.punchline: A parting shot designed to demean Pawnee's park project — delivered while fleeing.
jokes.explanation: A functional parting insult. The fact that it's delivered while fleeing adds comedy, and it's a crisp line that lands as an extension of the Eagleton condescension joke. Not exceptional but does its job well.

dialogue.speaker: Preston
dialogue.line: The palm trees were planted by the town's founder in 1912 as a symbol of Eagleton's superiority and refinement.

dialogue.speaker: Preston
dialogue.line: They thrive here because God chose Eagleton as his favorite town in Indiana.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head: 'They call their boogers Pawnee caviar.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining how Eagletonians view Pawneeans in the wake of the insulting presentation.
jokes.punchline: The specific, gross, and very specific allegation — boogers called 'Pawnee caviar' — is the kind of detailed grievance that implies Leslie has been collecting these slights for years.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy joke. 'They call their boogers Pawnee caviar' is five words of absurdist specificity that imply a whole cultural dynamic — Eagleton's contempt, Leslie's knowledge of it, and the slightly surreal nature of the rivalry. The gross specificity ('boogers') contrasted with the fancy term ('caviar') is a perfect word-level joke. Highly quotable. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what, Wreston? You're a big idiot! And your face is stupid!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm gonna throw things at this fountain and yell about you!

jokes.text: Leslie's revenge plan: 'I know what we're gonna do. We're gonna find out where he lives. We're gonna drive to his house. We're gonna set it on fire and watch it burn.' Ben: 'Leslie, we can't do that.' Leslie: 'You're right. We can't.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is furious about the insulting Eagleton park presentation and wants revenge.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's revenge fantasy escalates to literal arson with calm specificity ('drive to his house... set it on fire and watch it burn'). Ben's gentle 'Leslie, we can't do that' and Leslie's immediate, sincere 'You're right. We can't.' implies she needed someone to say it out loud.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy showing Leslie's rage leading to genuinely violent ideation that she immediately accepts as impractical when gently told. The 'watching it burn' detail is a nice escalation. Ben's minimal intervention ('we can't do that') and its immediate success is funny in its simplicity.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'll have the eggs, but I want them folded like an origami crane. And can you make the toast into a little edible shoe?

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: So... eggs and toast?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, yes, but with the specific presentation I—

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Eggs and toast. Coming right up.

jokes.text: Andy helps locate the lost child Joey. Andy tells Joey's relieved mother 'Just doing my job, ma'am.' Joey thanks Andy. Andy: 'Thank you, too, miss Hitler.'
jokes.setup: Andy has successfully reunited Joey with his mother and is receiving gratitude.
jokes.punchline: Andy, still in a version of the Bert Macklin mindset, thanks 'Miss Hitler' in front of Joey's completely confused mother — the roleplay bleeding into the real world.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed callback. 'Thank you, too, miss Hitler' — said earnestly in front of a civilian — lands because of the context gap: Andy is wrapping up the Bert Macklin fiction while the mother has no idea what's happening. The mother's 'What?' and Andy's blithe 'Don't worry about it' are perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Tom, you gotta understand something about business. You need swag.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Swag? Like confidence?

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: No man, literal swag. Promotional items. You know, branded merchandise. I once started a business called 'Swag' and it was just me stealing stuff and giving it away.

jokes.text: April's talking-head about Andy: 'Wow. You made those losers very happy.' Andy: 'Oh, no, I didn't. Bert Macklin did.' April: 'No...' Andy: 'FBI.' April: 'Actually, Bert Macklin kinda made that little boy cry.'
jokes.setup: April is crediting Andy for helping the lost child, but Andy deflects the credit to Bert Macklin.
jokes.punchline: April patiently notes that Bert Macklin is in fact responsible for the child crying — distinguishing between Andy's good act (finding the child) and Bert Macklin's bad act (terrifying him).
jokes.explanation: Good callback that wraps up the Bert Macklin arc. The distinction between Andy's genuine heroism and Bert Macklin's causing the child to cry is a funny and accurate character note. April's 'Actually, Bert Macklin kinda made that little boy cry' is perfectly flat delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Wreston
dialogue.line: She's smart, beautiful, passionate about her work. She cares deeply about this town and the people in it. She's dedicated, driven, and she makes everyone around her want to be better.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait... are you talking about me?

dialogue.speaker: Wreston
dialogue.line: Yes.

jokes.text: April's talking head: 'Seriously, I think Andy Dwyer makes a better real cop than Bert Macklin. Maybe it's time for Bert Macklin to hang up his shades.'
jokes.setup: April reflects on the afternoon's events
jokes.punchline: April — who was just enthusiastically playing 'Judy Hitler' in the role-play — delivers a deadpan suggestion that the fictional Bert Macklin retire, treating the character as real
jokes.explanation: Nice callback talking head. April treating Bert Macklin as a real agent who should consider retirement — while being the one who just played his love interest — is charmingly consistent with her character. The 'hang up his shades' phrasing is a good comic touch.

dialogue.speaker: Wreston St. James
dialogue.line: I've spent a lot of time in Pawnee. I know this town inside and out.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Oh my God, because of me, right? You came here because of me?

jokes.text: Andy's talking-head: 'Well, he's a rogue agent who refuses to play by the rules. Seriously, I think Andy Dwyer makes a better real cop than Bert Macklin. Maybe it's time for Bert Macklin to hang up his shades.'
jokes.setup: Andy is processing the criticism that Bert Macklin frightened a child.
jokes.punchline: Andy refers to himself in the third person as 'Andy Dwyer,' treating the Andy/Bert Macklin split as a genuine dual identity, and sincerely considers retiring his alter ego's 'shades.'
jokes.explanation: Andy treating himself and Bert Macklin as genuinely separate entities — to the point of evaluating 'Andy Dwyer' as a better cop than 'Bert Macklin' — is a beautiful character-specific joke. The retirement of the 'shades' as a formal ceremonial act is funny in its specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Bert Macklin gave everything for this country. He lost his left arm, his right leg, and most of his internal organs. But you know what? It was worth it.

jokes.text: Leslie meets Wreston at his office. Ben asks: 'Can I ask you, how are there palm trees here?' Wreston: 'Well, Eagleton lies on top of a hot spring which creates a micro-climate zone. We are... truly blessed.'
jokes.setup: They are inside what appears to be a pleasant, unusual space.
jokes.punchline: Wreston's explanation — 'Eagleton lies on top of a hot spring' — is delivered with the gravity of a religious fact, concluded with 'We are... truly blessed.' — the pause and the word 'blessed' elevating municipal geography to divine providence.
jokes.explanation: The pause before 'truly blessed' and the dead seriousness of its delivery make this land. Wreston's oblivious self-congratulation about geological fortune as though it's a virtue is exactly the Eagleton character comedy the episode has been building.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, check out my new office setup. I got a mahogany desk, Italian leather chair, and a view of the parking lot.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Really? I thought it looked pretty good.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's ostentatious, wasteful, and completely unnecessary. It's exactly the kind of thing I despise.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So... that's bad?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's the perfect small business aesthetic. You're going to make a fortune.

jokes.text: Leslie bursts in mid-apology montage and douses Wreston with a drink, shouting: 'Revenge! Ha ha ha! This is for Pawnee, you butt-faced pompous jerk! Whoo! I love you, Ben. Pawnee forever! You want a stupid tie? I'll give you a stupid tie!'
jokes.setup: Ben has been talking with Wreston. Leslie was supposed to be pursuing a reconciliation.
jokes.punchline: Leslie explodes into the room delivering what she believes is righteous revenge — a full attack on Wreston including a battle cry, liquid-dousing, and tie-stealing — declaring love for Ben in the process.
jokes.explanation: 'Butt-faced pompous jerk' as a carefully constructed insult, the mid-attack declaration of love for Ben, and the tie theft are all great character details. The comedy is amplified because this revenge is entirely misdirected — Wreston fired the people responsible. The physical comedy of the revenge sequence and Leslie's warrior cry are peak Leslie energy. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We're having a pizza party! And it's going to be amazing because I found a way to make it even cheaper.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We're spending less than Elon Musk spends on Twitter per second.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'You want a stupid tie? I'll give you a stupid tie. Ha ha! Wreston, suck it.' — then immediately Ben tells her Wreston is innocent
jokes.setup: Leslie is mid-revenge attack on Wreston, who is bewildered
jokes.punchline: Her triumphant 'Wreston, suck it' is immediately deflated by Ben's 'He didn't do it' — mid-victory lap
jokes.explanation: Well-structured reversal joke. The timing of Ben's revelation interrupting Leslie's victory is precise, and 'Wreston, suck it' is a satisfying escalation of the revenge language before the rug-pull. The double reversal — Leslie attacking, then learning she's wrong — is good comedic structure.

jokes.text: Leslie's full revenge attack ends. Ben tells her: 'He didn't do it, and he fired the people who did.' Leslie: [implied deflation/mortification]
jokes.setup: Leslie has just executed a full revenge attack on Wreston.
jokes.punchline: Ben delivers the information that undoes the entire attack — Wreston is innocent, the people responsible were fired. All of Leslie's righteous revenge energy has been spent on the wrong person.
jokes.explanation: The cringe payoff of the revenge scene. The structure — Leslie's elaborate attack immediately deflated by Ben's calm correction — is a classic sitcom structure executed well. High structure score. The comedy is in the timing and what we imagine Leslie's face doing.

jokes.text: Tom's 'pizza party' accountability: 'Attention, please. I've been going over the books, and I'm missing $9. Now, I'm not angry at whoever took it. Just come forward. You'll be served with a lawsuit, and we will move on with our lives.'
jokes.setup: Tom is addressing his Rent-A-Swag team with a financial discrepancy.
jokes.punchline: Tom's opening 'I'm not angry' is immediately contradicted by promising a lawsuit — the performative calm masking genuine litigious fury is perfect Tom Haverford.
jokes.explanation: Tom performing mature management ('I'm not angry') while immediately threatening legal action over $9 is beautiful character comedy. The amount ($9) is perfectly chosen — litigiously small. 'We will move on with our lives' as a post-lawsuit vision is both grandiose and sad.

jokes.text: Ron invites Tom to breakfast and orders for himself: '12 eggs, uncooked, and some toast. 20 slices, untoasted, in a row in a bag.' Tom: 'You want a carton of eggs and a loaf of bread.' Ron: 'Yeah, just the pancake breakfast is fine.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Tom are at a diner. Ron orders breakfast.
jokes.punchline: Ron's order — raw eggs and untoasted bread, specified with bizarre precision — is decoded by Tom as simply a carton of eggs and a loaf of bread. Ron's immediate capitulation to the pancake breakfast implies the whole elaborate order was performance.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The specificity of '12 eggs, uncooked' / '20 slices, untoasted, in a row in a bag' is absurd precision that Tom immediately translates into grocery items — revealing Ron's 'order' as just a weekly shopping list read to a waiter. Ron's instant pivot to pancakes is perfect. Near-maximum character integration — this is quintessential Ron Swanson. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Ron to Tom, mid-advice: 'Don't offer to pay if you're gonna be cheap.' Tom: 'But your swagger and your showmanship and your confidence is part of you... you can't have Rent-A-Swag without the swag.'
jokes.setup: Ron is counseling Tom on his new business approach.
jokes.punchline: 'You can't have Rent-A-Swag without the swag' is a perfectly logical tautology that lands as genuine wisdom — which itself is funny because it's a business name truism masquerading as mentorship.
jokes.explanation: The Ron-as-mentor dynamic is consistently good, and 'you can't have Rent-A-Swag without the swag' is a solid tautological piece of advice. Ron saying 'don't offer to pay if you're gonna be cheap' as fiscal wisdom is also a good character line. Competent comedy.

jokes.text: Ann reveals the team chipped in to help Tom: 'We all chipped in. Use it to spruce up the store. And in return you can give us like one share of stock in the company. Like a mini public offering.' Tom: '"Smort", Ann. Smort.'
jokes.setup: Ann offers Tom financial help and suggests they receive stock in return.
jokes.punchline: Tom praises Ann with 'Smort' — his intentional mispronunciation/portmanteau of 'smart' — delivered as though it's a real word and a genuine compliment.
