jokes.explanation: 'Smort' is a perfect Tom Haverford verbal tic — inventing slang that sounds like an error but is entirely intentional, delivered with total confidence. Maximum economy (one word) that captures his character.

jokes.text: Tom, enthused by Ann's investment, calls for: 'Waiter! Eight strips of bacon, uncooked, in a sealed package.'
jokes.setup: Tom is so excited he wants to celebrate. He calls to the waiter.
jokes.punchline: Tom mirrors Ron's absurd diner order from earlier — ordering raw, packaged bacon to celebrate — revealing he's absorbed Ron's peculiar approach to restaurant ordering.
jokes.explanation: A clean callback to Ron's absurd ordering — Tom unconsciously replicating Ron's pattern in his excitement. 'Eight strips of bacon, uncooked, in a sealed package' as a celebratory order is funny precisely because it's Ron's logic applied to Tom's energy. Good callback construction.

jokes.text: Wreston: 'I've never met two people more passionate about their hometown.' Ben: 'Oh, I'm actually from Minnesota.'
jokes.setup: Wreston compliments the pair's devotion to Pawnee
jokes.punchline: Ben matter-of-factly reveals he's not from Pawnee at all — he's from Minnesota — puncturing the romantic framing
jokes.explanation: Good timing joke. Ben's flat correction — he's not from here — delivered at the moment of maximum Pawnee-pride sentiment is a well-timed deflation. Economy is excellent. The comedy is all in the rhythm and the 'Oh' that opens Ben's line.

jokes.text: Wreston presents the park design: 'I've never met two people more passionate about their hometown.' Ben: 'Oh, I'm actually from Minnesota.' Leslie: 'Why do you know so much about Pawnee?' Wreston: 'Well, I'm in love with a woman from here. A strange, passionate, goof ball of a woman.' Leslie's talking-head: 'Me. He's in love with me.'
jokes.setup: Wreston is complimenting the passion for Pawnee he's witnessed.
jokes.punchline: Ben undercuts his own inclusion by noting he's from Minnesota. Wreston reveals his motivation is love for a Pawnee woman. Leslie's immediate talking-head clarification — 'Me. He's in love with me.' — is delivered as though this might not be obvious, which is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Multiple good beats: Ben's 'I'm actually from Minnesota' deflating the compliment, Wreston's romantic motivation reveal, and Leslie's talking-head clarification ('Me. He's in love with me.') treating the obvious as breaking news. The talking-head is the best beat — implying Leslie needed to announce this for the benefit of doubters.

jokes.text: Andy's elaborate Bert Macklin retirement ceremony: 'I'm sorry to see you go, Macklin. You didn't always play by the rules, but damn it, you were a hell of an agent. Today I say good-bye to the only life I've ever known... 40 years undercover. I never even met my family.'
jokes.setup: Following April's suggestion that Bert Macklin retire, Andy stages a full farewell ceremony.
jokes.punchline: Andy delivers a sincere, dramatic retirement speech for his own fictional alter ego — '40 years undercover. I never even met my family.' — with genuine pathos for a character he invented today.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout moments. Andy treating Bert Macklin's retirement as a genuine, solemn ceremony — 'the only life I've ever known,' '40 years undercover,' 'I never even met my family' — for an alter ego invented this afternoon is peak Andy character comedy. The escalating pathos he genuinely feels is both absurd and, through Andy's sincere delivery, somehow touching. Strong across all dimensions. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: April offers a retirement gift on behalf of 'the boys.' Andy: 'And this is all I have to show for it? Totally worth it.'
jokes.setup: April presents Andy/Bert Macklin with a (presumably small or silly) retirement gift.
jokes.punchline: Andy's initial deflation ('This is all I have to show for it?') immediately reverses to sincere satisfaction ('Totally worth it') — accepting the meager gift as adequate recompense for '40 years undercover.'
jokes.explanation: Andy's instant pivot from disappointment to full acceptance ('Totally worth it') is perfectly in character — his emotional simplicity is endearing and funny. The pause between the two sentences is the joke. High character integration and economy.

jokes.text: '40 years undercover. I never even met my family.' / 'And this is all I have to show for it?' / 'Totally worth it.'
jokes.setup: The Bert Macklin retirement ceremony continues with Andy delivering reflections from Macklin's career
jokes.punchline: Macklin's career tragedy — 40 years undercover, never meeting his family — is resolved with an immediate, sincere 'Totally worth it,' which is both funny and oddly touching
jokes.explanation: Good escalation within the retirement bit. The tragedy-to-instant-acceptance arc is perfectly paced. 'Totally worth it' — delivered without hesitation after 'I never even met my family' — is a genuinely funny payoff that also captures Andy's character: he finds no reason to dwell on regret.

jokes.text: April, playing a fellow agent at the retirement ceremony, delivers the closing line: 'If you ever need me, you know where to find me -- in bed next to you, probably having sex with you.'
jokes.setup: April is playing a colleague of Bert Macklin's at his retirement ceremony, delivering the standard 'if you ever need me' speech.
jokes.punchline: The stock retirement speech closer — 'you know where to find me' — deviates immediately into April breaking character to note she is literally in bed with Andy, 'probably having sex with you.'
jokes.explanation: A superb joke on multiple levels. April commits to the bit — the formal retirement-ceremony phrasing — then breaks its logic completely with the most specific, personal answer possible. 'In bed next to you, probably having sex with you' is simultaneously a relationship joke (April and Andy are married), an absurdist non-sequitur, and a perfect April-ism that uses the ceremonial format to deliver an intimate irreverence. Maximum character integration. One of the episode's top three. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: New Rent-A-Swag reveal: Tom has decorated the store and announces '30% more swag.' He adds: 'I took everything I own in my house and brought it here, except for my bed. I basically live here now.'
jokes.setup: Tom is unveiling the renovated Rent-A-Swag with the investment money.
jokes.punchline: Tom's swag-enhancement strategy was to donate all his possessions to the store — 'except for my bed' — meaning he now essentially lives in his shop.
jokes.explanation: Tom's desperate dedication — sleeping at the store, keeping only his bed — is both sad and funny, and very true to his character. The '30% more swag' guarantee is also a good mock-retail joke. The '16:15 — I basically live here now' beat reveals Tom's sacrifice with Tom's characteristic spin on it.

jokes.text: Ron inspects the new store: 'I hate all of this, which probably means it's good for your business.'
jokes.setup: Tom has revealed the renovated store and is seeking approval from his colleagues.
jokes.punchline: Ron offers a backhanded endorsement — his hatred of Tom's aesthetic is itself evidence that Tom's target market will love it.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect Ron Swanson line. Maximum economy, maximum character integration — Ron's aesthetic sensibility (masculine, minimal, functional) is the perfect negative indicator for a teenage fashion rental business. His self-awareness that his own hatred is a market signal is characteristically smart-in-an-unexpected-way. 'I hate all of this, which probably means it's good for your business' is an all-time Ron Swanson quote. Justifies near-top score.

jokes.text: Chris reveals his woodworking project was 'for displaying shoes!' Ron's response: 'Yes. That was always the plan.'
jokes.setup: Chris has just realized what the 'staircase to nowhere' design was for — it's a shoe display.
jokes.punchline: Ron claims 'that was always the plan' — implying the seemingly absurd design had a practical purpose all along. The comedy is in whether we believe him, and whether it matters.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback resolution. 'That was always the plan' is funny in its total commitment — Ron either did plan this, or is retroactively taking credit, and both options are perfectly Ron. The stairs-to-nowhere becoming a shoe display is an absurdist resolution that feels like a Ron Swanson lesson.

jokes.text: Tom announces 'Pizza Party! Part Two.' Reveals two pizzas. With toppings. 'Only on half. I'm not Zuckerberg.' / 'Eat up, chumps.'
jokes.setup: Tom is rewarding his team again, this time with an upgraded pizza party.
jokes.punchline: Two pizzas instead of one — but toppings only on half — with Tom citing Zuckerberg as the upper limit of generosity, then addressing his team as 'chumps.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback escalation. The pizza party has upgraded from: one small cheese-less pizza → two pizzas with toppings on half. The specific half-topping qualification and 'I'm not Zuckerberg' as the ceiling of his generosity is beautiful Tom Haverford comedy — 'Eat up, chumps' as a warm send-off makes it even better. Strong callback structure and character integration. Justifies 8+.

tmdb_overview: Leslie and Ben meet with an architect from their rival town, Eagleton, about designs for a new park.
insight: Solid character work drives a mid-tier episode with steady laughs, no standouts.
